title: The System of Professions: An Essay on the Division of Expert Labor
author: Andrew Abbott

dom.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field

st.t: Professional authority: AI enters an already contested field
st.an: Abbott supplies the cluster’s central mechanism: professional change occurs through contested control of work and jurisdictional competition, not straightforward technical substitution. His comparative legal history materially strengthens the framing by showing that lawyers’ authority was already contested by corporations and the state. The source does not itself predict AI-driven change, so its contribution is theoretical and historical rather than a verified AI forecast.
qs: I argue that control of work is central to professional development.

kp.k: Historical framework, not direct evidence of AI's effects
kp.d: This record concerns Abbott's 1988 theory of professional development, based on comparative historical study of nineteenth- and twentieth-century England, France, and America. The book is not held: the argument map synthesises publisher materials, Abbott's companion 1986 abstract, passages quoted by later works, and scholarly reception. Its reference to contemporary AI is an application noted by the record, not an empirical AI finding by Abbott.
qs: The book itself is not on file.
The argument map is labelled as such — it is a synthesis of those held materials plus the book's standard scholarly reception, not captured text.
Through comparative and historical study of the professions in nineteenth- and twentieth-century England, France, and America, Abbott builds a general theory of how and why professionals evolve.

kp.k: Control of work drives interprofessional competition
kp.d: Abbott's 1986 abstract, reproduced in the record, challenges approaches centred on professional structures and organisations. He argues that control of work, and competition between professions for that work, determine professional development. The record presents the 1988 book as extending this argument beyond law to expert labour generally.
qs: generally emphasized professional structure and organization while ignoring work and its control. I argue that control of work is central to professional development. Since work is central and since professions compete for it, interprofessional competition is the determining fact in the history of professions.
The book generalises that claim beyond law to expert labour as such.

kp.k: Professional practice comprises diagnosis, inference, and treatment
kp.d: The record identifies three acts of professional practice: diagnosis organises client information within professional knowledge; inference connects knowledge, client characteristics, and uncertainty to treatment; treatment supplies results or a prescription. The quoted wording is attributed to Abbott 1988, pages 40, 41, 44, and 48, as quoted in Faulconbridge, Sarwar & Spring 2024, not verified directly against the book. Academic knowledge supplies and legitimates the abstractions used in practice.

Alongside these sits academic knowledge, which legitimates and supplies the abstractions practice draws on.

kp.k: Professional jurisdiction is claimed, negotiated, and potentially partial
kp.d: The argument map presents jurisdiction as a claim linking a profession to work, made before audiences and resolved through settlements rather than naturally given ownership. It attributes the enumeration of lesser settlements—subordination, division of labour, intellectual jurisdiction, and advisory jurisdiction—to reception literature. Separately, the record quotes Faulconbridge et al. 2026 interpreting Abbott as tying jurisdiction to individual professionals' ability to claim diagnostic, inferential, and treatment expertise.
qs: The link between a profession and its work is a **claim**,   not a fact of nature.
the reception literature standardly enumerates subordination, division of   labour, intellectual jurisdiction, and advisory jurisdiction as the lesser settlements.

the jurisdiction of a profession is shown by Abbott   (1988) to be tied to the way individual professionals can claim the expertise needed to diagnose,   infer, and treat when encountering a client's needs.

kp.k: Jurisdictional exclusion makes professions an interdependent system
kp.d: The record's synthesis explains that exclusive control of tasks links professions competitively: gains by one profession entail losses by another. Technologies and organisational changes can create or eliminate task areas and trigger further adjustments across the system. These are theoretical mechanisms in the argument map, not measured effects of contemporary AI adoption.
qs: Because full jurisdiction is exclusive, professions are   interdependent: one profession's gain of task territory is another's loss.
new technologies and new organisational forms prominent among them

kp.k: Abstraction enables professions to defend and expand jurisdiction
kp.d: The argument map identifies abstraction as the mechanism by which professional knowledge systems redefine problems and tasks and claim new work. It qualifies the relationship as requiring optimal rather than maximal abstraction; more abstraction is not presented as unconditionally better.
qs: The Mechanisms of Jurisdiction Shift: Abstractions

only a knowledge system   governed by abstractions can redefine problems and tasks and annex new ones, so the (optimal,   not maximal) abstraction of a profession's knowledge decides what it can defend and take.

kp.k: Internal structures and external environments shape jurisdictional competition
kp.d: The record summarises three sets of conditioning forces: internal stratification, careers, client differentiation, and workplace organisation; social forces that open or close jurisdictions and change audiences and available powers; and cultural changes in knowledge, legitimacy, and universities. These are dimensions of Abbott's theoretical account, not findings about particular AI-era staffing, training, or pricing arrangements.

kp.d: The record describes the lawyers case study as addressing potential jurisdictional conflicts and complaints about unqualified practice and other invasions. It links the chapter's complaint-data method to Abbott's held 1986 article and attributes the comparative finding to that article: corporations were American lawyers' chief competitors, whereas the state was British lawyers' chief competitor. The supplied record gives no sample size or narrower observation period for this finding.

kp.k: Cross-professional histories illustrate changing task territories
kp.d: The record identifies two additional extended histories: information professions, covering librarians, accountants, and qualitative and quantitative task areas; and the construction of a personal-problems jurisdiction contested by clergy, neurologists, psychiatrists, and psychotherapists. It notes that the information-professions case is commonly applied to computing and now AI, while the personal-problems case ends with clergy surrendering jurisdiction. These are historical and interpretive framework materials, not forecasts of legal-sector outcomes.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The record contains no direct Abbott claim about AI. Its relevant claims concern competition for control of expert work and changes in professional jurisdiction.
pts.d: In Abbott's 1986 abstract reproduced in this record, he argues that control of work and interprofessional competition drive professional development. The record's synthesis of the 1988 book describes professional jurisdictions as interdependent and technologies and organisational changes as disturbances that can open or destroy task areas. It also attributes to the book an account of abstraction as a mechanism for defending or extending jurisdiction. These are general claims about professions, not predictions about AI replacing lawyers. The connection to contemporary AI is supplied by the record's scholarly framing rather than captured book text.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence basis is comparative historical research, accessed here through a structured secondary record rather than the full book.
pts.d: The publisher describes historical comparisons across England, France and America. The record identifies extended cases involving information professions, lawyers and their competitors, and professions contesting personal-problems work. It reports that the legal case uses complaints about unqualified practice and other incursions, and links it to Abbott's 1986 finding that corporations were American lawyers' chief competitors whereas the state was British lawyers' chief competitor. The argument map draws on the table of contents, publisher description, companion abstract and scholarly reception. Only four short passages defining professional acts are page-anchored quotations from the book, transmitted through Faulconbridge, Sarwar & Spring 2024. No AI performance or adoption evidence is offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account is historical and conditional, not an AI forecast with a specified horizon.
pts.d: The book was published in 1988 and addresses nineteenth- and twentieth-century professional development. In the record's synthesis, the claim that jurisdictional gains imply losses is qualified by the exclusivity of full jurisdiction; settlements can also involve less than exclusive control. Jurisdictional change depends on disturbances, audiences for professional claims, workplace and social conditions, and the capacity of professional knowledge to redefine tasks through abstraction. The record specifies optimal rather than maximal abstraction. It supplies no timetable for AI-driven change.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The affected groups are competing professions and the organisations contesting control of their work, including lawyers, corporations and the state.
pts.d: The framework concerns who gains, retains, shares or loses control of expert tasks. Its legal comparison distinguishes American lawyers' competition with corporations from British lawyers' competition with the state. Other cases concern librarians, accountants, clergy, neurologists, psychiatrists and psychotherapists. Internal stratification, client differentiation, workplace structure and career patterns also enter the account of jurisdictional competition. The record does not identify particular legal firm segments, junior-lawyer employment effects, client savings or access-to-justice consequences attributable to AI.
